locator: preamble, 'A non-cognitivist, however, may seek to explain how the attitudes or prescriptions expressed in moral claims are justified. (See Hare 1981, Campbell 1985, Gibbard 1990, and Blackburn 1998 for theories of moral justification compatible with non-cognitivism [...].) Indeed, an expressivist may invoke a deflationary conception of truth to support the idea that we can speak of justified moral beliefs that are “true” — without implying that justified moral beliefs accurately represent moral reality.'
interpretation: Read as the expressivist's available answer to how we know moral truths: moral 'knowledge' is justified attitudes, called true in the deflationary sense (DEF-TRUTH-MINIMAL), with no claim to represent moral reality. The entry says an expressivist 'may' take this line and cites Blackburn 1998 and Gibbard 1990 among theories of justification compatible with non-cognitivism; it does not say these texts put it in exactly these words. Recorded as quasi-realism's answer because the deflationary truth it invokes is quasi-realism's minimal truth (SEP-MORAL-COGNITIVISM §1.1). Attribution reading on a secondary witness: the claim records the option the entry reports, not a thesis of the entry's author. No primary text is pinnable (in copyright, no immutable open text).
